title: Take a seat
subtitle: When a town council decided to remove its old benches, the residents came up with another idea.
text: Three years ago, the council in the small market town of Pellbridge announced that forty of its wooden benches were to be taken away. Most were more than fifty years old, their paint was peeling, and several had lost a leg or a plank. {1} Within a fortnight, a petition to save them had been signed by more than two thousand people, roughly a third of the town's population.

The petition was started by Maureen Tolley, a retired postwoman who had walked every street in Pellbridge twice a day for thirty-one years. She knew the benches better than anyone, she says, because at one time or another she had rested on most of them. {2} Her solution was simple: if the council could not look after the benches, the people who used them would.

Under the scheme Tolley proposed, any resident, family or group could adopt a bench for a small yearly fee. In return, they agreed to keep it clean, repaint it when necessary and report any serious damage. {3} The council, perhaps relieved to have found a cheap way out of an unpopular decision, agreed to a twelve-month trial.

All forty benches were adopted within a month, and what happened next surprised even Tolley. The bench outside the primary school was covered in the painted handprints of every child in Year 2. One outside the fire station turned bright red overnight, complete with a small brass bell. {4} A knitting group dressed the arms of theirs in woollen sleeves, which have to be replaced every winter.

Not everyone approved. A few residents complained that the town centre now looked 'like a fairground', and one letter to the local paper described the benches as 'an embarrassment to the town'. {5} Almost all of them defended the benches, and several came from people asking how they could adopt one of their own.

The benefits have gone beyond appearance. Because adopters visit their benches regularly, damage is noticed and repaired far more quickly than it used to be. {6} Arthur Collins, who adopted the bench outside the library, now has lunch on it every Tuesday with a neighbour he had hardly spoken to in twenty years.

The trial ended two years ago, and the scheme is now permanent. Twelve new benches have been added, each of them adopted before it was even put in place, and three nearby towns have sent people to find out how it works. Tolley, who adopted the bench at the top of Station Hill, still sits on it most mornings. 'People think it's about benches,' she says. 'It isn't really. It's about having a reason to stop.'
sentences: Adopters would also be free to decorate their bench in any way they liked, as long as it remained safe to sit on.
That letter, however, produced more replies than anything the paper had printed in years.
Replacing them, the council explained, would cost far more than it could afford.
The council insisted, however, that every bench must be painted the same dark green as before.
Another, adopted by a retired sailor, was given a ship's wheel and a sign announcing its new name: the Good Ship Rest.
More unexpectedly, many adopters say the scheme has changed how well they know their neighbours.
She also knew who used them: the old man who fed the ducks, the parents waiting outside the school, the teenagers with nowhere else to go.
why: 'Them' are the worn-out benches; the cost of replacing them explains the decision, and the 'petition to save them' follows.
'She also knew' builds on knowing the benches; 'who used them' leads to 'the people who used them would'.

'Also' adds a further rule to the adopters' duties, and decorating 'any way they liked' prepares for the next paragraph. D tempts here, but it contradicts the red bench, the handprints and the ship's wheel that follow.
'Another' continues the list after the fire-station bench; 'theirs' then introduces one more adopter group.
'That letter' is the one calling the benches 'an embarrassment'; 'almost all of them' are its replies.
'More unexpectedly' moves beyond repairs; Arthur Collins and his neighbour are the example of knowing neighbours better.
